facts.title: A Name Older Than Latin
facts.text: Silver's chemical symbol Ag comes from the Latin word argentum, which itself traces back to a Proto-Indo-European root meaning 'shining' or 'white'. The English word 'silver' has a completely separate Germanic origin, which is why the symbol looks nothing like the modern name. Humans have known and worked silver for at least 6,000 years, making it one of the seven 'metals of antiquity'.

facts.title: The Best Conductor on Earth
facts.text: Silver has the highest electrical conductivity of any element, edging out even copper and gold. It is also the best thermal conductor among metals and reflects about 95% of visible light, the highest reflectivity of any metal. These records are why silver is used in high-end electrical contacts, mirrors, and specialized circuitry despite its cost.

facts.title: Forged in Colliding Stars
facts.text: Silver is not made in ordinary stars during their normal lives; most of it is created in violent cosmic events like supernova explosions and neutron-star mergers through rapid neutron capture (the r-process). Every silver atom in a ring or coin was literally cooked in a stellar catastrophe billions of years ago. Astronomers can detect silver's spectral fingerprint in the light of distant stars to study how the element spread through the galaxy.

facts.title: A Country Named After It
facts.text: Argentina is the only country named after a chemical element, taking its name from argentum because early European explorers believed the region held vast silver wealth. The nearby Río de la Plata, or 'River of Silver,' reflects the same hope. Ironically, most of the silver Spain extracted from the Americas came from Bolivia and Mexico, not Argentina itself.

facts.title: It Kills Microbes
facts.text: Silver ions disrupt the membranes and enzymes of many bacteria, which is why silver has genuine antimicrobial properties recognized by modern medicine. Silver-impregnated dressings are used today to treat burns and chronic wounds, and silver coatings appear on some medical catheters. Before refrigeration, people sometimes dropped a silver coin into milk or water to slow spoilage, an early practical use of this effect.

facts.title: The Soul of Photography
facts.text: For over a century, photography depended on the light-sensitivity of silver halide crystals such as silver bromide. When light strikes these crystals, it triggers a chemical change that can be developed into a visible image, the basis of every classic black-and-white photograph and X-ray film. At its peak, the photographic industry consumed a huge share of the world's silver supply before digital sensors took over.

facts.title: Why Silver Tarnishes
facts.text: That dark film on old silverware is not rust; silver does not react with oxygen easily. Instead, it reacts with trace sulfur compounds in the air, especially hydrogen sulfide, to form black silver sulfide on the surface. This is why silver tarnishes faster near sources of sulfur like rubber bands, eggs, or polluted air, and why a gentle electrochemical bath with aluminum foil can reverse it.

facts.title: Soft Enough to Shape by Hand
facts.text: Pure silver is remarkably soft and malleable, ranking only about 2.5 to 3 on the Mohs hardness scale, similar to a fingernail's resistance to scratching. A single gram can be drawn into a wire roughly two kilometers long. Because pure silver dents and bends so easily, jewelers harden it by alloying it with copper to create sterling silver, which is 92.5% silver.

facts.title: Money You Could Spend
facts.text: Silver served as money across countless civilizations, and its monetary legacy survives in language: the British 'pound sterling' and several currencies literally trace their names to silver weights. The biblical 'thirty pieces of silver' and the Spanish 'pieces of eight' were real, widely circulated coins. For much of history, silver was the everyday currency of trade while gold backed only the largest transactions.

facts.title: A Stable Pair of Isotopes
facts.text: Naturally occurring silver is a near-even mix of two stable isotopes, silver-107 and silver-109, present in almost equal amounts. This unusual balance gives silver an atomic weight of about 107.87. The decay of an extinct radioactive isotope, palladium-107, into silver-107 in ancient meteorites helps scientists date events from the first few million years of the solar system's formation.
